blocks: The Churning Sea & The Little Horn: The 1,260 Years to Judgment
The four predatory beasts, the church-state horn, the 1,260-year supremacy, and the pre-advent heavenly court.
Big idea

Daniel 7 shows four beasts, then a little horn, a power that rises among ten horns and rules for 1,260 prophetic years (prophetic years here means 1,260 days on the year-day scale, where one day stands for one year of real history). After that, and before Christ returns, Heaven holds a court — the court this sitting calls pre-advent, meaning it meets before the Advent, that is, before Christ comes back. The court rules in favor of God's persecuted people, and the Son of Man (the title Jesus took for himself) receives a kingdom that will never end.

In Sitting 6, Daniel faced the lions' den rather than surrender his daily prayer toward Jerusalem to an unchangeable Medo-Persian decree. God dispatched His angel to shut the lions' mouths, demonstrating God's deliverance of Daniel's prayer. The sealed pit and dawn deliverance are an illustration beside the sealed tomb (Daniel 6:17; Matthew 27:62–66; 28:1–6). The point of that comparison is the pattern. A sealed stone and a decree that could not be changed did not keep God's servant in the dark. The God who brought Daniel up out of the pit raised Jesus out of the tomb. Now, in chapter 7, the book turns from stories about the court to visions full of symbols, and it retells the four-kingdom prophecy of Daniel 2 with fierce animals.
Introduction
The Night Vision and the Winds of War
Daniel 7:1–3 · the first year of Belshazzar (Daniel 7:1)

In the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon, Daniel received a terrifying nocturnal revelation upon his bed (Daniel 7:1). Chapters 1 through 6 are historical narratives. They show God's sovereignty through the trials of His exiles. Chapter 7 begins the second half of the book. These are visions full of symbols, called apocalyptic visions, and they unfold world history from Daniel's day to the end of time.

Daniel beheld the "great sea" (the Mediterranean basin, the theater of ancient world empires) churned into foaming fury by "the four winds of the heaven" (Daniel 7:2). The same water is both a real sea and a picture. It is the sea Daniel knew, the one those empires bordered, and Scripture uses water for the nations themselves, so the tossing of that sea stands for the upheaval of the peoples around it. Scripture explicitly defines its own symbolic vocabulary:
Scripture interprets its own symbolic vocabulary

The Sea / Waters: Represent densely populated human civilizations, multitudes, and nations. Revelation 17:15 explicitly confirms: "The waters which thou sawest... are peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues" (see also Isaiah 17:12–13).

The Winds: Represent military warfare, political strife, and violent upheaval. Jeremiah 49:36–37 records: "And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them... for I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies" (see also Zechariah 7:14).

The Beasts: Represent world-ruling geopolitical empires arising out of human conflict. The interpreting angel declares: "These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth" (Daniel 7:17). Verse 23 then names the fourth beast "the fourth kingdom upon earth." Kings and kingdoms are the same chain.
The Horns: Daniel 7:24 says the ten horns are ten kings: "And the ten horns out of this kingdom are ten kings that shall arise" (Daniel 7:24; Revelation 17:12).

From this storm-tossed sea of warring nations, four massive predatory beasts emerged in succession. The dream of Daniel 2 had shown the same four kingdoms as one statue: a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay (Daniel 2:32–33). This vision retells the same historical sequence Nebuchadnezzar saw in the metal statue of Daniel 2. But it tells it with a contrast that matters. Pagan kings see their empires as glorious statues of gold and silver. Heaven sees them as vicious beasts, tearing and devouring the human family.

How do we know which empire each beast stands for? Scripture shows it. Daniel 7 retells the dream of Daniel 2 in a new picture, so it has the same four kingdoms in the same order, and Daniel 2:38 names the first one as Babylon. A later vision then confirms the middle two by name: in Daniel 8:20–21 the ram is Media and Persia, and the goat is Greece. So the beasts are Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and then a fourth kingdom that comes after Greece, which this course reads as Rome. Put the two pictures side by side and the chain matches metal for metal: gold is Babylon, silver is Medo-Persia, bronze is Greece, and iron is Rome. The divided feet, iron mixed with clay, match the ten horns of the fourth beast, the stage where the little horn rises (Daniel 2:41–43). The method behind all of this has a name: the historicist reading, which takes these visions as one unbroken line of real history from Daniel's day to the end, with each symbol standing for an actual kingdom or power. That is the reading this sitting follows.
Main Point 1
The Four Predatory Beasts: Succession of World Empires
Daniel 7:4–7
The four beasts arise from the sea in strict chronological succession, corresponding precisely to the four world empires that ruled the Mediterranean world:
1. The Winged Lion: The Neo-Babylonian Empire

The first beast was like a lion with eagle's wings (Daniel 7:4). The lion—the king of beasts—and the eagle—the king of birds—depict the imperial majesty and speed with which Nebuchadnezzar conquered the ancient Near East. Two prophets had already used those same two animals for that empire. Jeremiah 4:7 pictures the coming conqueror as a lion from the north, the direction Babylon lay from Jerusalem. Habakkuk 1:6–8 describes the Chaldeans sweeping down like an eagle. The Chaldeans are the Babylonians who ruled from the city of Babylon. Babylon's own art used lions and winged guardian creatures too, so the picture fits the power the prophets had already named. Daniel watched until the wings were plucked, the beast was lifted from the earth, made to stand on two feet like a man, and a man's heart was given to it. This vivid symbol, as one reading — the verse itself does not say this — recalls Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation in Daniel 4: after living like an animal, he lifted his eyes to heaven, acknowledged the Most High, and was restored (Daniel 4:32–37).
2. The Lopsided Bear: The Medo-Persian Empire

The second beast was like a bear, raised up on one of its sides, with three ribs clenched between its teeth (Daniel 7:5). The bear represents the heavy, lumbering, massive armies of Medo-Persia. It was raised up on one side because the Persian wing of the dual monarchy emerged far stronger and more dominant than the Median wing. Here is why ribs could stand for conquests: the beast is commanded, "Arise, devour much flesh" (Daniel 7:5), and ribs are the picked-over remains of what a beast has already eaten, so the ribs picture nations already swallowed. This reading names the three principal conquests that forged the Medo-Persian Empire: Lydia (547 B.C.), Babylon (539 B.C.), and Egypt (525 B.C.). The verse does not name them; the names come from dated history, not from a line in Daniel 7:5, and the command to devour much flesh describes the vast territorial expansion of the Persian kings.
3. The Four-Headed, Four-Winged Leopard: The Grecian Empire

The third beast was a leopard possessing four wings of a fowl on its back and four heads (Daniel 7:6). A leopard is naturally swift; a leopard with four wings signifies unmatched speed. Between 334 and 331 B.C., young Alexander the Great conquered the entire Persian Empire with breathtaking speed, marching thousands of miles across Asia Minor, Egypt, and Mesopotamia before his death at age 32. Following Alexander's sudden demise in 323 B.C., his empire was not bequeathed to his young heirs, but after decades of civil warfare among the Diadochi, it was partitioned among his four leading generals: Cassander (Greece and Macedonia), Lysimachus (Thrace and Asia Minor), Seleucus (Syria and Mesopotamia), and Ptolemy (Egypt and Palestine). Within a few decades the four realms were reduced to three major kingdoms, but the vision pictures the first division. These four divisions correspond to the four heads of the leopard.
4. The Dreadful and Terrible Beast: The Roman Empire

The fourth beast was so monstrous and unnatural that no animal in nature could depict it: it was "dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it" (Daniel 7:7). This corresponds to the iron legs of Daniel 2, representing the iron monarchy of imperial Rome. With ruthless military efficiency, Rome crushed the Hellenistic kingdoms, crucified Jesus Christ, destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 70 A.D., and governed the Mediterranean world. The beast had ten horns (Daniel 7:7). The verse does not name them. This reading takes them as the ten kingdoms that took over the Western empire after its collapse in A.D. 476: the Alemanni, the Franks, the Anglo-Saxons, the Burgundians, the Visigoths, the Suevi, and the Lombards, together with three that were later uprooted, the Heruli, the Vandals, and the Ostrogoths (Main Point 2).
Main Point 2
The Emergence of the Little Horn: The Church-State Counterfeit
Daniel 7:8, 20–25

While Daniel was contemplating the ten horns on the head of the fourth beast, he witnessed an astonishing development: an eleventh horn, small at first, began to sprout up among them (Daniel 7:8). This "little horn" power is the primary antagonistic focus of Daniel 7. Scripture provides a precise, cumulative profile of this power, one identifying mark after another, like the counts in a courtroom charge:

"I considered the horns, and, behold, there came up among them another little horn, before whom there were three of the first horns plucked up by the roots: and, behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of man, and a mouth speaking great things." — Daniel 7:8 (KJV)
The eight biblical identifying marks of the Little Horn
Geographic and Chronological Origin (7:8): It rises out of the fourth beast (Western Rome) among the ten horns, meaning it emerges during the disintegration of Western Rome following 476 A.D.

Diverse from the Ten (7:24): The verse says this horn is "diverse" from the other ten, but it does not say in what way; that step is the reading's, not the verse's words. This reading takes the difference from what the horn does. It speaks words against God, wears out the saints, and tries to change God's law. Those are acts of religion carried out with civil force, while the horns it rises among are ordinary kingdoms. In plain words, this horn is a church and a civil power joined together, and the marks that follow are what that difference looks like.

Uproots Three Horns (7:8, 24): Three kingdoms stood in its way. The Heruli fell in 493 and the Vandals in 534. The Ostrogoths withdrew from Rome in 538; they retook the city in the 540s and were not fully defeated until about 553. These three Germanic nations held Arian Christianity, a rival confession, and opposed the bishop of Rome. The claim is that the three kingdoms in his way lost their place: two fell earlier, and the third left Rome in 538 and was fully defeated about 553. So the 1,260 years start in 538, the year the third kingdom let go of Rome, while the third kingdom's final defeat came about 553: the start of the span and the fall of the third horn overlap at the edges instead of landing on one day.
Eyes Like the Eyes of a Man (7:8): Eyes in Scripture denote wisdom, vision, and discernment (Ephesians 1:18). The eyes point to insight, intelligence, and foresight.

A Mouth Speaking Pompous Words Against the Most High (7:8, 25): It utters blasphemies against God, arrogating to an earthly office titles that belong to Christ (such as Vicar of Christ) and claiming prerogatives that belong to God alone, such as the power to forgive sins (Mark 2:7).

Persecutes and Wears Out the Saints (7:21, 25): It wages institutional warfare against faithful believers who adhere to Scripture, using civil power, inquisitions (church courts set up to try people accused of wrong belief), and crusades to suppress dissent through centuries of persecution. Two of the groups named in the diagram are the Waldenses, a reforming movement of the Middle Ages, and the Huguenots, a reforming movement in France in the 1500s. Both were tried and executed as heretics, that is, as people condemned for holding beliefs the church rejected. This reading counts them among the saints the horn wore out.

Thinks to Change Times and Laws (7:25): The Aramaic words zimnin (times) and dath (law) name an intent to change appointed times and law. In plain words, the verse says this power intends to change God's appointed times and his law. The Ten Commandments are also called the Decalogue, a name that means ten words. Of the Ten Commandments, the fourth is the one about a time: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy" (Exodus 20:8). So the time this reading names is the Sabbath, which this reading says the church-and-state power taught Christians to keep on Sunday instead of the seventh day. A later catechism, a teaching book of questions and answers, that joins the command about images to the first command, and splits the last command in two, is the further picture this sitting offers of that change.
Reigns for a Measured Prophetic Span (7:25): It exercises civil supremacy for "a time and times and the dividing of time"—a span systematically demonstrated below to equal 1,260 solar years.

Daniel 7's little horn is the historical papacy: the office of the bishop of Rome in its church-state role, where religious and civil authority were joined. This is a claim about an institution and its historical exercise of authority, not a judgment about Roman Catholics as individuals. Many Catholics sincerely follow Christ, and disagreement over this interpretation gives no warrant for prejudice or hostility toward them. The quotation below records the harsh words Martin Luther wrote about the papal office. It is kept here as a historical source; it is not a statement about Catholic believers today.

"This teaching shows forcefully that the Pope is the very Antichrist, who has exalted himself above, and opposed himself against Christ because he will not permit Christians to be saved without his power, which, nevertheless, is nothing, and is neither ordained nor commanded by God." — Martin Luther, Smalcald Articles (1537), Part II, Art. IV
Three other answers, and why the text does not fit them

Some readers give the little horn a different name, and some say the numbers are only pictures. Here are three other answers. For each one: what it claims, why a person might hold it, and why this course says the text does not fit it.

Antiochus IV (the preterist answer, the reading that puts the fulfillment in the past). This view makes the horn a Greek-Syrian king of the second century B.C. Why a reader might hold it: Antiochus really did persecute the Jewish people and defile the temple, and tying the vision to him lets the prophecy speak to the people who first read it. Why this course says it does not fit: Daniel 7:23–24 puts the little horn on the fourth beast, "out of this kingdom," and says it rises after the ten horns. Daniel 8:20–21 names the ram as Media and Persia and the goat as Greece, so Greece is the leopard, the third beast. Antiochus ruled one part of Greece, so he belongs with the third beast, not the fourth. The ending does not fit either. When the horn's time is over, the judgment sits and the saints receive "an everlasting kingdom" (Daniel 7:26–27). No such kingdom followed Antiochus's death in 164 B.C.

One future antichrist (the futurist answer, the reading that puts the fulfillment in a still-future crisis). This view makes the horn a single man who rules for three and a half literal years at the very end, after a long gap. A seven-year form of it calls that final crisis the tribulation, meaning a time of great suffering, and calls a last-days league of nations eschatological, meaning belonging to the last days. Why a reader might hold it: the Bible does speak of a final crisis before Christ returns (Daniel 12:1), and a short crisis under one ruler is easy to picture. Why this course says it does not fit: the horn comes up among the ten horns, and the ten horns are "out of this kingdom," the fourth kingdom (Daniel 7:24). This course reads them as the kingdoms that grew out of Rome's division, the same stage Daniel 2 shows as the feet. Daniel 2:41 calls the feet the same kingdom, divided, not a new one that appears after a wait. Daniel 7 gives no sign of a pause between the beast and its horns. The vision runs on in order: beast, horns, little horn, judgment, kingdom. A modern version that reads the horns as today's great powers, or as a last-days league of nations, meets the same wall: the horns belong inside the fourth kingdom's own breakup, not to a stage added after it.

The picture-only answer. A third reading says the beasts and the numbers are pictures of a spiritual struggle, with no dated history behind them; it is sometimes called the allegorical or poetic reading. An allegory is a story whose details stand for something else, and on this reading the court scenes are that kind of picture. Why a reader might hold it: the chapter is full of symbols, and readers have watched people misuse Daniel's numbers, so it is easy to conclude that no number here is meant to be counted. One form of it ties the court scene to the church council held at Nicaea in A.D. 325, where the church set out its statement of belief about who Christ is, as if the vision were a dramatization of that meeting. Why this course says it does not fit: Daniel 7 does not leave the symbols to the reader. The angel defines them — four kings (Daniel 7:17), a kingdom (Daniel 7:23), ten kings (Daniel 7:24) — and the vision runs in order from Babylon to a kingdom that never ends. A picture with no history behind it leaves the worn-out saints with nothing dated to stand on, and it turns a verdict into a mood.

The short-span answer. Some read the three and a half times as three and a half literal years in the second century B.C., during the persecution under Antiochus IV (about 167 to 164 B.C.), and call it a local crisis rather than a long age. Why a reader might hold it: that persecution was real, and a short local crisis is easy to picture. Why this course says it does not fit: the horn of Daniel 7 rises on the fourth beast, the one that comes after Greece. The same span appears in Revelation as forty-two months and 1,260 days (Revelation 12:6, 14; 13:5). That reads like a measured age, not a weekend.
In plain words: the horn grows out of Rome's divided kingdoms. It belongs after Rome, in the Christian centuries, not before Rome and not thousands of years after it.
Main Point 3
The 1,260-Year Prophetic Timeline (538 to 1798 A.D.)
Daniel 7:25; Revelation 12:6, 14; 13:5

Scripture provides the time given into the little horn's hand: "they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and the dividing of time" (Daniel 7:25). Rather than guessing at this period, Scripture interprets its own arithmetic through parallel prophetic books:
Building the 1,260-year prophetic calculation

Step 1: Calculate the Prophetic Units: In biblical Aramaic and Hebrew, a "time" (iddan) represents one prophetic year of 360 days (the ancient biblical calendar; Genesis 7:11, 24 and 8:3–4 show 5 months equal to 150 days, so each month had 30 days and twelve months make 360). • "A time" = 1 prophetic year = 360 days • "Times" = 2 prophetic years = 720 days • "The dividing of time" = 1/2 prophetic year = 180 days • Total: 1 + 2 + 1/2 = 3 1/2 prophetic years, which is 1,260 prophetic days.

Step 2: Confirming Parallels in Revelation: Revelation uses three interchangeable phrases to describe this identical span of persecution: • "A thousand two hundred and threescore days" (Revelation 12:6). • "A time, and times, and half a time" (Revelation 12:14). • "Forty and two months" (42 × 30 = 1,260 days; Revelation 11:2; 13:5).

Step 3: The Year-Day Principle: Scripture supplies the day-for-a-year scale: "each day for a year" (Numbers 14:34) and "I have appointed thee each day for a year" (Ezekiel 4:6). On its own that scale does not prove the principle, so here is why this reading applies it here. In this vision the four beasts are four kings (Daniel 7:17), the fourth beast is called a kingdom (Daniel 7:23), and the ten horns are ten kings (Daniel 7:24). The time given in the same vision belongs to the same picture, so it is symbolic too. A literal three and a half years would be a very short career for a power that rises among ten kings, wears out the saints, and tries to change times and laws (Daniel 7:24–25). So the days stand for years. Sitting 0 introduced this scale, and Sitting 9 tests it on the seventy weeks. Read that way, the 1,260 prophetic days represent 1,260 literal calendar years of rule by a church-state power.
On the year-day scale, this sitting charts a 1,260-year envelope in European history. The papacy’s civil rise was gradual; no single headline marks every transition — but two dates mark the period:
The historical boundaries: A.D. 538 to A.D. 1798

The starting point (A.D. 538): In A.D. 533, Eastern Roman Emperor Justinian wrote to Pope John II recognizing the Bishop of Rome as head of all the churches. That letter is the decree the diagram names, and one name will do for it here: Justinian's recognition. That recognition could not take effect in Rome while the Ostrogoths, one of the three rival kingdoms, held the city under siege. In 538 the Byzantine general Belisarius broke the Ostrogothic siege of Rome, so the way was open. This reading starts the 1,260 years there. It is a chosen marker, not a year Daniel prints: the Ostrogoths retook Rome in the 540s and were not fully defeated until about 553.

The Concluding Anchor (A.D. 1798): Adding 1,260 years to 538 lands on 1798 (538 + 1,260 = 1798). The French Revolution — the upheaval in France that toppled its monarchy and stripped the church of its place in the state — struck at papal power. On February 15, 1798, General Berthier declared Rome an independent republic and captured Pope Pius VI. The pope lost his rule over Rome and was taken prisoner. Here is why this reading marks the end of the span there: the horn's civil power means rule over a state, and when the pope lost Rome and was taken prisoner, that rule was gone. His rule was later partly restored and finally lost in 1870, which is why this reading calls 1798 the end of the prophetic period and not the end of the papacy. This reading treats it as the end of the little horn's civil power, the prophetic "deadly wound" (Revelation 13:3).

Main Point 4
The Pre-Advent Heavenly Court: Ancient of Days and the Opened Books
Daniel 7:9–12, 26

Daniel 7 gives an order of events. First the little horn rules and wears out the saints (Daniel 7:21, 25), which this reading dates to 538–1798. Then Daniel's eyes are drawn upward to a court in heaven (Daniel 7:9–10). Finally the horn is destroyed and the saints receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:26–27). So the court comes after 1798 and before Christ returns to earth, and that order is kept everywhere in this sitting. In plain words, the court gives the verdict and the return brings the possession. The Ancient of Days gives the kingdom to the Son of Man (Daniel 7:14), and the saints are named in the same grant, for the kingdom "shall be given to the people of the saints of the most High" (Daniel 7:27). They enter it when Christ returns and possess it for ever (Daniel 7:18, 22; Daniel 2:44). So when a table in this sitting speaks of the kingdom being awarded to the saints, it means the verdict the court gives; when it speaks of the saints receiving the kingdom, it means the day they enter it. One answer, two moments: the decision in heaven, then the possession on earth. Here is the court:

"I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened." — Daniel 7:9–10 (KJV)
Court vs. Stone: Two distinct moments of reckoning

A critical error in prophetic interpretation is to confuse the heavenly courtroom of Daniel 7:9–14 with the Second Coming of Christ (the stone striking the statue in Daniel 2:34–35). They are two distinct, sequential phases of divine judgment:

Phase 1: The Court Sits in Heaven, Before Christ Returns (Daniel 7:9–14): Thrones are placed, the Ancient of Days sits, and the books of record are opened. Notice the timing: the court sits while the little horn is still speaking great words (Daniel 7:11). The horn's civil power ended in 1798, but its great words did not stop: a claim to speak for God does not need an army, and this reading holds that the horn still speaks them while the court sits. Daniel 7:22 says that "judgment was given to the saints of the most High," which this reading takes to mean that the court rules in favor of God's people. The Son of Man is brought to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and a kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14).

Phase 2: The Verdict Is Carried Out at the Second Advent (Daniel 7:26–27; Daniel 2:44): The court takes away the horn's dominion "to consume and to destroy it unto the end" (Daniel 7:26). Christ returns to earth, and the saints possess the everlasting kingdom with him (Daniel 7:18, 27). Daniel 7 does not give dates for the court's beginning or end; Sitting 8 dates its start at 1844. The court is the trial in heaven; the Second Advent is the carrying out of the sentence on earth.

Main Point 5
The Redemptive Climax: The Son of Man Crowned Before the Father
Daniel 7:13–14, 27; Matthew 26:64; Hebrews 7:25
As Daniel watched the heavenly court in session, he witnessed the glorious climax of redemption history:

"I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed." — Daniel 7:13–14 (KJV)

Note the direction of Christ's movement with utmost care: the Son of Man does not come down to the earth. He comes with the clouds of heaven TO the Ancient of Days, moving into the immediate presence of God the Father inside the celestial courtroom. Jesus Christ enters as our High Priest (the priest who stands before God for the people), our Advocate (the one who speaks for another in court), and our Representative (the one who stands in our place) (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1). Standing before the Father and the unfallen angels (the angels who never sinned), Christ presents His own perfect righteousness and atoning blood on behalf of His persecuted people. Here is why his blood is the answer the court needs: the books are records of real lives and the charge against the saints is real, so the answer must be real too, and his sacrifice is that answer.

During His earthly trial before the high priest Caiaphas, Jesus took up the words of Daniel 7:13, identifying Himself as this very Son of Man: "Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" (Matthew 26:64). The earthly high priest tore his robes, but Christ was pointing beyond the earthly court to the supreme court of heaven where He reigns as King. Notice what those words do and do not say. In Daniel 7:13 the coming with the clouds is a coming to the Ancient of Days, and that is the scene Jesus claims here: the throne, the right hand of power, the court above every earthly court. His visible return to earth is spoken of elsewhere, where He comes with power and great glory (Matthew 24:30) and every eye sees Him (Revelation 1:7). First the court in heaven, then the appearing on earth.
In plain words: the little horn's reign has a measured end, heaven's court sits, and the kingdom is given to the Son of Man who stands for his people.
INTERPRETATION

Daniel 7 answers a question Daniel 2 left open. The statue showed four kingdoms and a stone. It did not say what happens to God's people while the fourth kingdom is still on the throne. Daniel 7 does.

The chapter shows the same four kingdoms from heaven's side, as four beasts. Then, among the ten horns of the fourth beast, a little horn rises. It speaks against God, wears out the saints, and is given a measured span: "a time and times and the dividing of time" (Daniel 7:25). On the year-day scale that is three and a half prophetic years, which is 1,260 years. So the persecution has a limit. That is the first thing this chapter says, and it says it before it says anything else.

The second thing is what happens when the limit is reached. A court sits in heaven, the books are opened, and the Son of Man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion, glory, and a kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). Read the order and it is clear. The horn rules for a set time. The court sits and decides. The horn is judged, and the kingdom is given to the one who stands in the believer's place.

That is why this chapter is not a puzzle about beasts. It is the answer to a believer who has watched the wrong side win for a very long time. The power that speaks against God is real, and its cruelty is real. But it operates on a clock, and the clock was set by the court that sits above it.

The bottom line is where you look for the verdict. Earthly courts may condemn the saints; the court in heaven vindicates them. The little horn has a beginning and an end. The kingdom given to the Son of Man has neither.
CHRIST

The Son of Man who approaches the Ancient of Days is Jesus Christ, our High Priest and Advocate. Earthly courts may condemn the saints, but the heavenly court vindicates all who trust in His blood. The Ancient of Days gives the Son of Man the kingdom (Daniel 7:14), and the saints share it with him (Daniel 7:27), a kingdom that can never be destroyed.
Practical Application
Living Under the Heavenly Verdict
Daniel 7 provides foundational anchor-points for every Christian facing ideological, legal, or spiritual pressure in a secular age:
1. Discern the spiritual battle behind political power

Human empires rise through violent conquest and arrogance, but God's people do not place their ultimate trust in earthly kings, political parties, or human legislation. Earthly kingdoms give way; the true kingdom belongs to the Son of Man. A way to practice this: name the power you are most tempted to trust this week, write down what you expect it to give you, and write beside it what only God's kingdom gives — a kingdom that cannot be destroyed (Daniel 7:14).
2. Stand firm on God's holy law and Sabbath

The little horn attempted to change God's times and law. The change this sitting names is the one about the Sabbath: a weekly day of worship moved from the seventh day to Sunday (Main Point 2, mark seven). When human religious traditions contradict the plain commandments of Scripture, believers must stand with the apostles: "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). The seventh-day Sabbath remains the enduring sign of the Creator's sovereignty.
3. Reject human mediators; cling to Christ alone

This reading points to the horn's titles, such as "vicar of Christ" (one who stands in Christ's place), and to confessing sins privately to a priest, which is called auricular confession, from the ear, because the sins are spoken into a priest's ear. Both belong to the fifth mark in the list: titles that belong to Christ, and the claim to forgive sins, which Scripture reserves to God (Mark 2:7). Scripture declares there is only one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Do not let any human priesthood stand between you and Christ. Go directly to his throne of grace.
4. Rest in the assurance of the open books

The heavenly judgment is good news for the believer. Christ does not enter the court to condemn His people, but to advocate for them, blot out their sins, and name them heirs of the everlasting kingdom, the kingdom they enter when he returns. With Christ as our Advocate, we face the opened books with peace, joy, and unfailing confidence.
The principle to remember
TEXT — Does Daniel 7:13 explicitly state that the Son of Man comes TO the Ancient of Days in heaven?
HISTORY — Are the 1,260 prophetic years verified from the lifting of the Ostrogothic siege in 538 A.D. to Berthier's capture of Pius VI in 1798 A.D.?
INTERPRETATION — Does Scripture interpret its own symbols: waters as peoples, winds as war, beasts as kingdoms, and horns as rulers?
CHRIST — Is Jesus Christ your heavenly Advocate who stands before the Ancient of Days to vindicate you in the judgment?
The Son of Man Vindicated Before the Ancient of Days

In Daniel 7, the terrifying panorama of predatory beasts and the 1,260-year blasphemous reign of the little horn culminates in a celestial courtroom of blinding glory. The Ancient of Days sits upon a flaming throne, the books are opened, and 'one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days' (Dan 7:13). This Son of Man is Jesus Christ, who repeatedly applied this very title to Himself during His earthly ministry, even declaring to the council, 'Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven' (Matthew 26:64).

The scene of Daniel 7:13 is not Christ coming to earth at His Second Advent; it is Christ moving into the presence of the Ancient of Days in the heavenly sanctuary to receive the kingdom, glory, and dominion. Daniel 7:11 has the horn's great words still spoken while the court sits. That heavenly judgment comes after the 538–1798 phase, not inside it. The KJV of Daniel 7:22 reads, 'judgment was given to the saints of the most High' — the saints receive the verdict and the kingdom, not a modern paraphrase smuggled into the verse as if it were the KJV wording.

Anchor your confidence in Christ's advocacy rather than earthly religious hierarchies or human mediators. There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). When you face spiritual persecution or feel worn out by the moral darkness of this age, remember that the judgment has been seated, the horn's dominion is taken away, and Christ will soon share His kingdom with those who remain faithful to His name.
